Corporate profits had reached a record $4.7 trillion for the last twelve months by mid-year. That’s a 17% increase on the previous year’s figures. Tax breaks contained in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act have led to a sharp drop in corporate tax receipts. Washington’s enormous fiscal deficit – running at around 6% of GDP – provides an economy wide fillip to corporate bottom lines. When it comes to individual companies, however, the surge is all about AI. Earnings per share for members of the S&P 500 Index (.SPX) were up 26% in the twelve months to July: the long-run average annual growth rate is 7%. Expected earnings for the third quarter are 35% above estimates from a year ago. Gerard Minack of Minack Advisors lists 19 members of the S&P 500 that are heavily involved in the AI buildout: Big Tech “hyperscalers”, chipmakers and supply-chain companies such as fibre-optic provider Corning (GLW.N) . Since January 2025, these “AI-19 stocks” have seen forecast earnings rise by around $700 billion, 50% more than all the other companies in the US stock market benchmark. Analysts at Morgan Stanley predict that 42 leading companies exposed to AI will grow their earnings by 67% in 2026. The aggregate earnings growth of the other S&P 500 companies is projected at 23%. Put another way, these 42 stocks account for more than half of the earnings growth for the S&P 500 in the current year. Next year Morgan Stanley expects the basket of AI plays to contribute 78% of the S&P 500 earnings growth as AI investment in the United States rises to a forecast $1.6 trillion. “This is the probably the most earnings accretive capex boom in history,” says Jefferies strategist Christopher Wood. AI capital spending inflates profits because, as Minack points out, one company’s capex is another’s revenue. Profits emerge because the investing company does not expense all its costs at once, whereas the seller of capital equipment immediately books the full amount as revenue. Buyers of Nvidia’s (NVDA.O) graphics processing units depreciate their purchases on average over around 6 years, while the chip giant books a juicy upfront profit. What’s more, when the buyer is acquiring chips for a data centre that is under construction, the depreciation clock does not start ticking until the facility is up and running. Morgan Stanley estimates that as much as 40% of this year’s AI capex will become operational sometime between 2027 and 2029. The earnings mirage will not last indefinitely, though. By the end of the decade, the hyperscalers’ annual depreciation charges will range between $500 billion and $1 trillion, according to a recent report from Capital Gearing Asset Management. Investments in unlisted AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are also super-charging profits. Tech giants reflect changes in the private market value of these investments in their earnings statements as “other non-operating income.” In the four quarters leading up to mid-2026, the four major hyperscalers – Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) , and Meta Platforms (META.O) – saw annualized earnings increase by $222 billion while "other non-operating income" rose by $224 billion. In other words, the rising value of unlisted AI investments accounted for all the increase in their reported earnings. The fact that the AI buildout is increasingly financed with debt adds a further element of instability. The hyperscalers will plough almost all their operating cash flow into capex in the current financial year. These companies have issued around $225 billion of unsecured bonds so far this year, equivalent to around 30% of their full-year capital spending. They also have lease commitments for $1.1 trillion of AI equipment and services, which, since they haven’t yet commenced, are not reported on their balance sheets. Next year, Morgan Stanley analysts forecast the hyperscalers will have negative free cash flow of around $550 billion. “Access to credit markets and the ability to absorb higher interest rates are fundamental for hyperscalers and neoclouds to be able to deliver against our capex estimates,” says the Wall Street bank. That shouldn’t be too much of a problem for giants like Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta which enjoy solid credit ratings because of their dominant positions in search, software, online retailing and social media. The economist Hyman Minsky applied the term “Ponzi finance” to businesses that do not generate sufficient cash flows to meet their outgoings. Loss-making data centre operators and AI frontier labs fit this description. Ponzi finance units, said Minsky, need rising valuations to raise additional capital. When valuations decline and the capital markets seize up, these shaky institutions collapse, causing losses to metastasise through the financial system. That is what happened in early 2000 after the credit markets lost confidence in the debt-fuelled buildout of the information superhighway. That investors are starting to question the viability of the AI investment splurge should come as no surprise. Productivity improvements from implementing the new technology remain elusive. Rogue AI agents are causing havoc. Models continue to hallucinate. Chinese AI companies are rapidly taking market share from the leading US AI labs. OpenAI has pushed back its planned IPO while upstart data centre operators such as [USN:L6N45V00W TEXT:"Firmus Technologies"] have shelved their stock offerings. Prospective investors in Anthropic are [USN:L6N46118I TEXT:"weighing a lower valuation"] for the AI company, Reuters reported citing four people familiar with the matter. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , the largest neocloud, has seen its [USN:L6N46113K TEXT:"shares and bonds tumble"]. The shares of hyperscalers and chipmakers do not look expensive relative to earnings. That’s because the bubble is in profits, not valuations. US homebuilders were in the same position at the peak of the housing bubble in 2006, as were global miners when the commodity supercycle came to a sudden stop in the middle of the last decade. When the AI capex boom ends, earnings growth could revert to trend, says Minack. That moment may come sooner rather than later. Follow @Breakingviews on X

item.title: Apple's foldable iPhone hits stores with $2,000 price tag and scarce supply
item.description: Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Christine Chen, Will Russell
item.content:encoded: Apple's (AAPL.O) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches. From Singapore and Shanghai to London and Berlin, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days. Competitors such as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones. It is also an early challenge for Apple's new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September. Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary". Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online. In Sydney, which was the first Apple store to sell the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT). "This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a 512GB Duo. In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to [USN:P8N44H02N TEXT:"six straight quarters"] of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices. Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi (1810.HK) , but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6 a.m. for Apple's first foldable. "I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said. Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models. Others were resellers. In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked. Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain. "Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said. MIXED REVIEWS Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers. But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple customers. "It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber. Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone." In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one. "I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices." TOUGH TO FIND Apple's entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC. IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast. "Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo. "Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said. ($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars) ($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

item.title: Trump says Musk restored Ukraine's Starlink access, declines to say if they spoke
item.description: Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Bogage , Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: Donald Trump said on Thursday that SpaceX (SPCX.O) CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access but the US president declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to the billionaire about the matter. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Thursday that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink. "I don't want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference, I guess. The bottom line - he put it back," Trump told reporters when asked if he spoke to Musk. Trump did not elaborate further. Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"hampered"] the country's attack and air defense drone missions against Russia. The Starlink system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, the WSJ reported earlier, citing US and Ukrainian officials. Some Ukrainian officials told the newspaper the system had not been restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said earlier on Thursday that speed on Starlink systems had not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the coming days. Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system's speeds remained capped, according to the newspaper. Trump has denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown. Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's [USN:L6N467096 TEXT:"access to Starlink"] were up to its parent company SpaceX and Musk, not the White House. Zelenskiy's relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskiy. Russia [USN:L1N4671BN TEXT:"pounded Kyiv"] with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. Trump had promised to end the war when he took office but the goal has remained elusive.

item.title: Steep bill for AI buildout punishes Meta, other tech favorites
item.description: The tab for the next round of the AI buildout came due on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf, Sudeshna Ghoshal
item.content:encoded: The tab for the next round of the AI buildout came due on Thursday. Investors sold shares of Meta Platforms (META.O) and a wealth of companies central to the AI trade, a day after Meta — one of the hyperscalers spending billions to build data centers and other infrastructure supporting the AI boom — said it would issue a new class of shares that will help it raise funds. Meta fell 7%, its largest drop since July. SpaceX (SPCX.O) declined 9% and semiconductor company Nvidia (NVDA.O) — a bellwether of the AI trade — dropped 4%. The Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 2.6%, its largest decline since June 5. Sentiment was also hurt by a 12% plunge in shares of semiconductor company Lam Research (LRCX.O) following its results. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index (.SOX) lost 6.7%. The pullback is the latest test for the AI trade as investors focus on the rising costs of long-term projects where the payoff remains uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, but Wall Street now expects that the rise in borrowing costs will motivate tech companies like Meta to sell billions of dollars in stock to fund the next round of building. That dilution could put pressure on share prices, and is a potentially unwelcome development when major US stock indexes remain near all-time highs despite a punishing month of volatile trading. RETURN ON INVESTMENT CONCERNS Selling started with "the big question about the (return on investment) on all the spending," said Matthew Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak. "It's just becoming more and more evident to people that it's going to take a lot longer." Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital LLC in New York, agreed that ROI concerns are central while also citing remarks by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about a financing bottleneck for smaller AI companies as contributing to the selling. Meta said on Wednesday it would use new Class C shares, which hold no voting power, to [USN:l4n4671s3 TEXT:"fund AI spending and other priorities"]. Meta also raised the low end of its annual spending forecast to $135 billion from $130 billion, with the high end unchanged at $145 billion. That level of spending will require lots of investor participation in coming stock sales. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. It was the first cash burn at Meta in more than a decade. “More spending, negative free cash flow, not enough revenue being generated from the spend (is) concerning investors that this is just sort of a bit of a money pit,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut. The action highlights concern over how AI investment will be paid for. Credit default swaps, which track perceived default risk for the debt of the biggest AI players, have largely risen over the past year, with Meta’s hitting a record on Thursday . INVESTOR ANXIETY SHOWS Fresh signs of market anxiety over AI spending snowballed into a broad market selloff Thursday, with some saying an AI pullback could hit US growth. Investors sought the safety of Treasury bonds, sending those prices higher . "This is your classic rotation day,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner, co-founder and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. “You can see the money going into Treasuries, so it's a classic safety move ... They are rotating out of techs, out of the AIs, and into the more safety trades, whether it's bonds or some of those big Dow Jones stocks.” Thursday’s selloff added to the pressure on the neocloud companies at the heart of the AI buildout, with Nebius (NBIS.O) off 7% after announcing a new $3.5 billion credit line from Citigroup and CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , whose unsecured bond yields soared to 15% in last week’s AI selloff, down 10%. Bank of America analyst Tal Liani said in a report on Thursday he is maintaining a buy rating and a price target of $140 on CoreWeave stock heading into next month’s earnings report, though he said he believes the firm will need to raise $20 billion to fund commitments to customers — the sort of prospect that is generating anxiety among tech investors. "Nobody is worried about Meta or Amazon or Google getting the financing they need," Maley said. "But if it gets prohibitive for smaller companies, then you don't have to have an implosion of things to make people nervous."

item.title: Blackstone sets up $10 bln test of banks’ AI risk
item.description: The buyout shop and co-owner Warburg Pincus want to sell IntraFi, which lets lenders offer deposit insurance beyond a statutory $250,000 cap. The mooted value represents 400% growth over seven years. It’s just awkward timing as fears rise of autonomous agents managing balances.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Gandel
item.content:encoded: Private equity is about to find out whether bankers should really be worried. Digital assistants like Meta’s (META.O) Muse threaten to upend lenders' businesses: if artificial intelligence can automatically move deposits to high-interest accounts, cheap balances might disappear. They could also theoretically mimic IntraFi, a company built entirely on cash-shuffling. Buyout shops Blackstone (BX.N) and Warburg Pincus want to offload the so-called reciprocal deposit network for $10 billion, [USN:L6N4651A1 TEXT:"Reuters reported"] on Tuesday. Such a big return could somewhat allay technological fears. IntraFi is not a bank, yet it [USN:L6N45N19E TEXT:"benefits from the same frictions"] that protect lenders’ deposit franchises. Thanks to consumer inertia, large banks get away with paying little or no interest on many accounts, which provides cheap funding to issue loans at far higher yields. Executives like JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon have brushed off concerns that so-called agents like Muse could automate away this cozy equilibrium. The new sale process offers a kind of test on how investors feel. Deposit juggling is IntraFi’s specialty. Depositors enjoy government-provided insurance in case their bank fails, but only up to $250,000 per account. That could make them leery of handing large sums over to any but the safest institutions. IntraFi's reciprocal network automatically splits and swaps deposits above the cap among member banks, creating linked accounts that each qualify for full insurance coverage. Lenders can then offer more protection to customers, paying a fee to IntraFi for the privilege. Agents could replicate that service on the customer end, sparing humans the labor of opening and tracking balances among multiple accounts. The threat is theoretical at this point. IntraFi's value is, in part, in retaining a single point of contact: a business can act as if they just work with one lender, which they might engage with for a range of services. On their own, a client would also have to do a lot of account-juggling to cover big sums. A number of banks, including JPMorgan (JPM.N) , have said they would restrict agents' access. As with any technology, though, improvements and rapid adoption would make it harder to keep saying no. A sale near the $10 billion target would suggest confidence that this won’t happen. Add on $4.8 billion of debt, according to S&P Global Ratings, and the price would equate to about 24 times IntraFi’s $630 million of annual EBITDA, as reported by Reuters. Given Blackstone's initial $2.5 billion investment in 2019 and nearly $3 billion of dividends along the way, it simplistically implies an over-400% increase in value. Regulatory loopholes are not easily closed, even by frontier technology. Follow Stephen Gandel on LinkedIn and X . Reuters [USN:L6N4651A1 TEXT:"reported"] on October 20 that Blackstone and Warburg Pincus had hired investment banks Morgan Stanley and Guggenheim Securities to find a buyer for IntraFi. The private equity firms are trying to sell their stakes for a combined $10 billion, according to the report. The company, which Blackstone acquired in 2019 for $2.5 billion, dominates the market for reciprocal deposits, which enable banks to spread their customers' money across multiple institutions in order to access federally backed insurance on balances exceeding $250,000. Warburg Pincus purchased a portion of Blackstone's IntraFi stake in 2022 for an undisclosed amount. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s designated first citizen
item.description: The Facebook founder doesn’t hide his admiration for Roman Emperor Augustus. An agreement allows him to sell new non-voting stock to pay a tax bill. Doing so, gives him a larger purse to pursue bigger dreams of conquest while retaining absolute control. Caveat emptor applies.
item.dc:creator: Robert Cyran
item.content:encoded: Mark Zuckerberg has never hid his obsession with Rome and emperor Augustus. A new agreement keeps Meta Platforms’ (META.O) first citizen in the $1.8 trillion company’s capital of Menlo Park, California for eight years. It also allows the founder, chairman and chief executive to pursue bigger dreams of conquest while retaining absolute control. Zuckerberg has some 60% of the company's vote because of Class B shares, which have 10 votes a piece. Yet his economic stake is far less at around 14%. A proposed California tax would hit billionaires like Zuckerberg for 5% of their wealth. He told Meta’s board he might move out of the Golden State, according to the New York Times. It’s understandable directors want the boss in California. Under his leadership, the Facebook and Instagram operator has grown from start up to one of the most valuable companies on earth. Zuckerberg’s focus may be on Meta’s big push into artificial intelligence, but having a leader around the office still delivers better results according to a study by researchers at Boston College and Arizona State University. The company will issue one non-voting Class C share for each existing share investors have. Zuckerberg can sell up to 20% of his immediately, and the remainder in steps, without reducing his voting power. In exchange he stays put instead of relocating out of state. It’s not obvious that Zuckerberg would actually move, let alone leave the company. His desire for retaining power reflects his care for the entity he built. The new shares will be useful for many things. Meta can use them to buy rivals, compensate workers, or raise money to invest in data centers. The company will need this ability, as its artificial intelligence push chews up resources. On Wednesday, the company said it burned over $2 billion in cash in the third quarter. Shareholders have revolted before. In 2017 the company abandoned an attempt to issue non-voting stock. What’s different today is the expensive race to dominate machine learning. Perhaps the opportunity is so big, and the increasing number of tech giants with non-voting stock like SpaceX (SPCX.O) , that equity owners will play along. Rome’s history, though, is hardly an endorsement of letting one person hold absolute power. If things start to go wrong, Meta’s ruler can essentially ignore plebeian investors. Follow Robert Cyran on Bluesky . Meta Platforms said on October 21 that the board had approved a new class of non-voting stock. All Class A and B owners would be issued one new Class C share for each share held. Founder, Chief Executive and Chair Mark Zuckerberg agreed to a deal wherein he can sell up to 20% of his Class C shares in exchange for a commitment to stay in California and remain head of the company for eight years. If he sells more of the shares, his voting stake will be reduced. The restriction on his remaining Class C shares will be lifted in steps over this period. Zuckerberg has a 60% voting stake and owns just over 13% of all shares. The company also reported third quarter results on October 21. In the three months ending September 30, the company had $2.1 billion of negative free cash flow. Meta’s stock fell 6% in early trading on the morning of October 22. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: U.S. climate champion Gina McCarthy honoured in Reuters Events Global Sustainability awards
item.description: Gina McCarthy seems remarkably chipper given the seemingly relentless opposition to climate action, led by her own government under President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Balch
item.content:encoded: Gina McCarthy seems remarkably chipper given the seemingly relentless opposition to climate action, led by her own government under President Donald Trump. McCarthy, who was head of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Obama administration, and White House climate adviser under Joe Biden, accepts that her view isn’t universally held. “It may sound a little crazy to people,” she says. “But I'm really bullish on what's happening next.” She spoke to The Ethical Corporation on the eve of Reuters Events Global Sustainability Awards, where she was honoured with a Lifetime Achievement award, in recognition of spending more than three decades “at the forefront of America's fight for cleaner air, safer water, and a liveable climate”. Her bullishness was also clear in her acceptance speech, which was delivered by video from her home outside Boston. “Despite all the nonsense from my federal government and their fossil fuel allies, there has been a massive surge this past year in clean energy,” she said, with state and local governments from across the U.S. “working together to drive a more aggressive energy transition ... with a relentless spirit of optimism”. McCarthy will be taking that optimistic spirit to next month’s United Nations’ climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, as chair of America Is All In , a coalition of pro-climate U.S. cities, states, corporations and community groups. Newly assembled solar panels at a new solar facility in Humble, Texas, US, October 6, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian “We don't want the rest of the world to think that the United States is what Trump says. The United States is what our state and local governments say,” she tells The Ethical Corporation. With the U.S. midterm elections, in the week prior to COP31, expected to restore the House of Representatives to Democratic control and weaken Republicans’ grip on the Senate, that message will be even easier to sell. She cites Illinois, which has passed legislation to add 3 gigawatts of battery storage to its grid by 2030, and California, which plans to modernise its already pioneering carbon credit programme. Cleveland, Ohio, meanwhile, is pursuing a new five-year plan to cut emissions by nearly two-thirds (against 2018 levels). Sceptics will note that all the examples derive from strongly Democrat-controlled constituencies, but McCarthy points out that the Republican stronghold of Texas is home to a substantial portion of the record additions of solar and battery projects added to the U.S. grid in the past year. McCarthy has long believed that for the average U.S. voter, economics trump ideology when it comes to powering their homes and businesses. A drone view shows California’s largest battery storage facility, as it nears completion on a 43-acre site in Menifee, California, U.S., March 28, 2024. REUTERS/Mike Blake The relative affordability of renewable power compared to fossil fuels makes it increasingly attractive to householders, in the face of a monthly inflation rate of 3.4%. Corporations, meanwhile, have been leaning heavily into renewable energy, mindful not only of rising energy costs but growing threats to energy security. According to the business-backed Corporate Energy Buyers Association (CEBA), corporate-sponsored clean energy projects in 2025 exceeded the total power generation of 45 individual U.S. states. With U.S. investment in the global clean energy transition now running at around $378 billion, it may seem like supporters of America Is All In, who collectively represent 63% of the U.S. population and 74% of U.S. GDP, can rest easy. Gina McCarthy pictured in Washington in 2014 as she arrives to sign a proposal under the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution from existing power plants. REUTERS/Joshua Roberts Yet having seen many of the environmental advances made under her watch rolled back by the Trump Administration, McCarthy is far from complacent. In mid-September, for example, the EPA, which she headed up between 2013 and 2017, said it planned to desist from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector. According to America Is All In, the proposed move could see a potential ten-fold increase in coal-fired power, with severe impacts on greenhouse gas emissions but also human health. “To have this (Clean Power Plan) arbitrarily taken off the books by this administration was absolutely ludicrous. It had nothing but benefits,” she says. Another policy reversal that she admits was “not easy” to watch was the scrapping of the EPA’s landmark 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding , barring the agency from tracking and capping emissions from cars and heavy-duty vehicles. But it was the dilution of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) that McCarthy deems the most consequential of all the Trump administration’s recent moves to halt transition efforts. Introduced in the wake of the COVID pandemic, the IRA earmarked around $485 billion in public spending and tax breaks for investments in healthcare, clean tech and other transition-related investments. Its dismantlement continues to incense McCarthy, who describes it as “one of the biggest opportunities that our country ever had” to provide U.S. citizens with clean, secure and affordable energy. A drone view shows Elon Musk's xAI Colossus 2 "Macrohard" data centre in Southaven, Mississippi, U.S., May 30, 2026. REUTERS/Kevin Wurm Yet her response is typically indefatigable. “You know, we all have to pull up our big boy, big girl pants when these challenges happen.” Fuelling her confidence are two fundamental convictions; namely, that people will be ultimately won over by clean power’s cost competitiveness, and will also realise that “this administration isn’t forever”. She takes heart from the multiple lawsuits now being brought by state authorities and campaign groups against various efforts by the Trump administration to weaken environmental protections. Earlier this month, a coalition of 25 cities and states – including New York, California, North Carolina and Washington D.C. – issued a petition to the U.S. court of appeals for the District of Columbia to review the EPA’s proposal to remove emission standards for power plants. Also encouraging is the spirit of cross-sector collaboration that is now emerging across the U.S. She points to the C40 Global Urban Data Centres Pact . A new mayor-led initiative endorsed by 49 cities, including 22 in the U.S., seeks to promote greater public accountability in the management of resource-hungry data centres. The pact, which includes Chicago, Austin, Seattle and Miami, comes on the back of increasing disquiet in the U.S. over the water and energy consumption of AI data centres. While McCarthy acknowledges the potential economic benefits of such facilities, she argues that companies and regulators have not paid enough attention at their environmental and community impacts. She would like to see tax revenues from data centres used to help fund renewable energy projects and community infrastructure. “They (data centres) are one of the fastest-growing challenges that we have in the United States,” she says. “There has to be a way to ensure that they can do their thing without destroying us.” Reuters Events Global Sustainability Awards 2026: other winners AI for Sustainability Excellence Award — Winner : Tracera; Highly Commended : Jupiter Intelligence Biodiversity Champion Award — Winner: Olam Agri; Highly Commended : Rainforest Expeditions Business Transformation Award — Winner : Pure Data Centres Group; Highly Commende d: Pandora Circularity Award — Winner : LIXIL Corporation; Highly Commended : Groupe SEB Data-driven Sustainability Communication Award — Winner : Syngenta Group; Highly Commended : Diversified Energy Company Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Award — Winner : Atlas Renewable Energy; Highly Commended : Halkbank Leadership in Water Stewardship Award — Winner : SPG Dry Cooling; Highly Commended : Nestle Waters & Premium Beverages Net Zero: Leadership Award — Winner : Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited; Highly Commended : Edison International Net Zero: Operations Transformation Award — Winner : Cushman & Wakefield and Standard Chartered; Highly Commended : Bodycote plc Net Zero: Supply Chain Decarbonisation Award — Winner : Schneider Electric; Highly Commended : AstraZeneca Partnership of the Year Award — Winner : Hindustan Unilever Limited; Highly Commended : Aviva Product Innovation Award — Winner : Hitachi Energy; Highly Commended : Fairphone Responsible Investor of the Year Award — Winner : Circulate Capital; Highly Commended : EFG Holding Rising Sustainability Star Award — Winner : Daniel Kopp; Highly Commended: Marine Sanouiller SDG Pioneer of the Year Award — Winner : Telkom Indonesia; Highly Commended : Sunbeth Global Concepts Ltd. item.description: Wall Street vue en baisse, l'Europe dans le rouge entre résultats, pétrole et dette française
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Wall Street vue en baisse, l'Europe dans le rouge entre résultats, pétrole et dette française 23 octobre (Reuters) - Wall Street est attendue baisse et les Bourses européennes reculent vendredi à mi-séance, la confiance des investisseurs restant plombée par les craintes budgétaires en France et par la flambée des prix du pétrole, tandis que la dernière vague de résultats d'entreprises entraîne de lourdes pertes pour certains grands noms de la cote tels que Kering, Safran ou Volvo Cars. Stellantis, Bolt et Grand Paris veulent lancer des services de mobilité autonome dès 2028 23 octobre (Reuters) - Stellantis, l'entreprise estonienne de VTC Bolt et la région Île-de-France prévoient de lancer un programme de conduite autonome dans la capitale française en 2028, en utilisant des véhicules du constructeur franco-italo-américain, ont-elles annoncé vendredi dans un communiqué commun. AmEx relève son objectif de bénéfice grâce aux dépenses de sa clientèle aisée 23 octobre (Reuters) - American Express (AmEx) a relevé vendredi son objectif de bénéfice pour 2026 après avoir publié de solides résultats au troisième trimestre de son exercice, tirés, une fois de plus, par les dépenses des clients fortunés. L'Oréal grimpe, la croissance au T3 illustre la résilience des cosmétiques 23 octobre (Reuters) - L'action L'Oréal était en nette hausse vendredi en milieu de matinée, le géant français des cosmétiques ayant publié la veille une croissance des ventes trimestrielles supérieure aux attentes, soulignant sa résilience dans un contexte de ralentissement du reste du secteur du luxe. Volkswagen: Les salariés menacent de faire grève si les accords salariaux ne sont pas respectés FRANCFORT, 23 octobre (Reuters) - Les dirigeants syndicaux allemands ont menacé d'organiser des grèves chez Volkswagen à partir de janvier, si l'entreprise ne revient pas d'ici fin octobre sur sa récente annulation des accords salariaux, marquant ainsi une escalade des conflits sociaux au sein du groupe. Kering chute de 10% après un nouveau recul des ventes de Gucci 23 octobre (Reuters) - L'action Kering dévisse de 10% vendredi, au lendemain des résultats trimestriels du géant français du luxe, marqués par une baisse des ventes de Gucci, sa marque phare, dans un contexte de faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins. Zone euro/PMI: La croissance décélère à son plus bas niveau depuis quatre mois, face à la hausse des coûts et aux turbulences en France LONDRES, 23 octobre (Reuters) - La croissance du secteur privé de la zone euro a ralenti en octobre pour atteindre son plus faible rythme depuis juin, sous l'effet d'une hausse des coûts liée à l'énergie et d'une nouvelle contraction en France dans un contexte de pressions politiques et financières, selon l'enquête PMI préliminaire publiée vendredi. Allemagne/PMI: La croissance de l'activité économique décélère en octobre BERLIN, 23 octobre (Reuters) - La croissance du secteur privé allemand a décéléré en octobre, les entrées de nouvelles commandes n'ayant que modestement augmenté, montrent les résultats préliminaires de l'enquête PMI publiée vendredi. Contraction inattendue de l'activité économique en octobre, les pressions politiques et financières pèsent PARIS, 23 octobre (Reuters) - L'activité économique française s'est contractée de façon inattendue en octobre, marquant un revirement rapide par rapport à la croissance enregistrée en septembre, montre l'enquête préliminaire publiée vendredi par S&P Global. GB/PMI: Les entreprises enregistrent leur meilleur mois d'activité depuis février LONDRES, 23 octobre (Reuters) - Les entreprises britanniques connaissent leur meilleur mois en termes d'activité depuis février, avec la hausse des nouvelles commandes et à la reprise de la demande liée à l'intelligence artificielle, selon l'enquête préliminaire des PMI de S&P Global publiée vendredi.

item.description: Tirs dans les Yvelines, un mort et quatre blessés, le Pnat saisi
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Tirs dans les Yvelines, un mort et quatre blessés, le Pnat saisi PARIS, 23 octobre (Reuters) - Un homme à bord d'un véhicule a tiré à l'arme automatique sur la voie publique vendredi à Trappes et La Verrière, deux communes des Yvelines, à l'ouest de Paris, faisant un mort et quatre blessés graves, avant d'être interpellé, a déclaré le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, qui va se rendre sur place. La tempête Austen balaie l'ouest de la France, 161.000 foyers privés d'électricité 23 octobre (Reuters) - Quelque 161.000 foyers étaient privés d'électricité vendredi matin dans l'ouest de la France balayé par la tempête Austen, la première de l'automne, qui s'accompagne de vents violents, rapporte Enedis. Macron annonce l'interdiction des manifestations "sans légitimité" Les autorités interdiront dans les prochains jours les manifestations et regroupements sans "légitimité" et proposeront des "tracés alternatifs" aux syndicats pour protéger les centre-villes, a annoncé jeudi Emmanuel Macron, à deux jours d'un nouvel appel à manifester émanant notamment des "gilets jaunes". France: Premier décès lié au virus Shamonda, aucun risque sanitaire à ce jour selon les autorités PARIS, 22 octobre (Reuters) - Un patient est décédé début octobre du virus de Shamonda, une première en France et dans le monde, a annoncé jeudi le gouvernement, ajoutant qu'il n'y avait à ce stade aucun risque sanitaire pour la population générale au vu des connaissances sur ce virus. Cisjordanie: Les oliveraies de Palestiniens pillées lors d'attaques violentes de colons israéliens LUBBAN AL-GHARBI, Cisjordanie, 22 octobre (Reuters) - Ému aux larmes en se remémorant l'attaque contre son oliveraie par des colons israéliens il y a environ deux semaines près du village palestinien de Lubban al-Gharbi, en Cisjordanie, Ahmed Salem a déclaré s'être retrouvé impuissant, craignant d'être agressé s'il tentait d'intervenir pour protéger son exploitation. Gaza: Trois Palestiniens tués par des frappes israéliennes selon les secours LE CAIRE, 22 octobre (Reuters) - Des frappes et des tirs israéliens ont tué au moins trois Palestiniens jeudi, dans deux incidents séparés survenus dans la bande Gaza, selon les autorités sanitaires locales. Serbie: La face autoritaire de Vucic en lumière avant les élections législatives BELGRADE, 22 octobre (Reuters) - - Le militant serbe Marko Marjanovic rentrait du supermarché à Belgrade lorsque des officiers masqués l'ont embarqué dans un véhicule avant de l'amener dans le sous-sol d'un commissariat de police où il a été maintenu à l'isolement pendant deux jours sous un éclairage intense. Un Ukrainien, soupçonné d'espionnage pour la Russie, arrêté en Allemagne 22 octobre (Reuters) - Un ressortissant ukrainien a été arrêté dans le nord-est de l'Allemagne, soupçonné d'espionnage au profit de la Russie, selon un communiqué publié jeudi par le parquet fédéral. France: Macron dénonce les commentaires des dirigeants étrangers sur les manifestations Emmanuel Macron a dénoncé mercredi les commentaires émanant de "dirigeants étrangers" en campagne électorale à propos des manifestations émaillées de violences du 17 octobre en France, à l'occasion d'une tournée dans les pays du Golfe. Les syndicats appellent à un grand mouvement le 5 novembre, mobilisation des Gilets jaunes samedi Les principales organisations syndicales appellent à un mouvement d'ampleur le 5 novembre - la CGT lançant même un mot d'ordre de grève générale - après avoir été reçus à Matignon par le Premier ministre, Sébastien Lecornu, pour faire le point sur la crise sociale qui secoue le pays.
